title: Emoji Movie Is Back and Better Than Ever
subtitle: Gene just wants to feel something. Turns out that's a lot to ask of a phone.
intro: The Emoji Movie came out in 2017, got destroyed by critics, made $217 million worldwide, and never once apologized for itself. Now it's back, and the conversation around it has quietly shifted. What looked like a cynical cash grab the first time around has developed a genuine cult following, the kind that watches it ironically and then watches it again without the irony. Gene is a meh emoji who can't do meh. That's the whole premise, and it holds up better than anyone expected it to.

items.name: T.J. Miller
items.bio: Miller voices Gene, the emoji who refuses to make one face. He plays the whole thing with an anxious sincerity that keeps the film from collapsing into pure product. Gene wants to fit in and keeps failing at it, which is a more relatable setup than it has any right to be.

items.name: James Corden
items.bio: Corden is Hi-5, a hand emoji who peaked and knows it. He latches onto Gene because he needs the attention, and the film is honest about that. Hi-5 is not a good friend. He is a very funny one.

items.name: Anna Faris
items.bio: Faris voices Jailbreak, a princess emoji who hacked her own code and refuses to go back. She has a goal that exists completely outside of Gene's story, which makes her the most functional character in the film.

items.name: Patrick Stewart
items.bio: Stewart plays Poop. He committed. That is the entire note.

quote: I'm not broken. I just feel everything.

whyWatch.body: Here is the thing about The Emoji Movie that nobody wanted to admit in 2017: the central premise actually works. An emoji who cannot control his expression, living inside a phone where conformity is the only survival strategy, is a real setup with real stakes. The film earns its ending because Gene's problem is specific, not vague. He doesn't want to be special. He wants to stop being wrong.
